summary: This standards-track memo describes using the Cryptographic Message Syntax to protect firmware packages, which contain code for hardware modules. A digital signature protects against undetected modification, and encryption can be used for confidentiality.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC says how to protect a firmware update using CMS, the container format used for signed email. The update is compressed, then encrypted, then signed, and the signature covers a set of facts about the package: which version it is, which devices it is for, and what it can do. The device checks that signature against a public key it already trusts before running anything.

subtitle: How to wrap a firmware update in signed, optionally encrypted CMS so a device only runs code from sources it trusts.

tldr.problem: A hardware module that loads firmware from a network or a memory device has no way to tell a genuine update from a tampered one, so a modified package could install code the vendor never wrote.
tldr.mechanism: The firmware package is wrapped in a CMS SignedData structure, optionally compressed and encrypted first, and the signature is made over a set of signed attributes that name the package, the hardware it is for and the algorithms it implements.
tldr.outcome: A module that holds a trust anchor can decide whether a package came from an acceptable source, refuse a package meant for other hardware, and refuse to roll back to a version with a known flaw, and the module can send back a signed receipt or error report.

today:
RFC 4108 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the document that describes using CMS to protect firmware packages.

The memo describes the format and the loader's duties, not a delivery method. It says so explicitly: it does not attempt to specify a physical interface, any related driver software, or a protocol for loading packages, and many different delivery mechanisms are envisioned, including portable memory devices, file transfer and web pages. What it does fix is the format that must be presented to the module whatever the interface.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document describes the use of the Cryptographic Message Syntax to protect firmware packages, and also the use of CMS for receipts and error reports for firmware package loading. CMS is a data protection encapsulation syntax that makes use of ASN.1. The protected firmware package can be associated with any particular hardware module, but the specification was written with the requirements of cryptographic hardware modules in mind, as these modules have strong security requirements.

The firmware package contains object code for one or more programmable components that make up the hardware module, and it is treated as an opaque binary object. It is digitally signed, and optional encryption and compression are also supported. When all three are used, the firmware package is compressed, then encrypted, and then signed. Compression reduces the size of the package, allowing more efficient processing and transmission. Encryption protects the package from disclosure, which allows sensitive firmware to be transmitted over insecure links, and the encryption algorithm and mode employed may also provide integrity, protecting the package from undetected modification. The encryption protects proprietary algorithms, classified algorithms, trade secrets and implementation techniques. The digital signature protects the package from undetected modification and provides data origin authentication, allowing the hardware module to confirm that the package comes from an acceptable source.

If encryption is used, the firmware-decryption key must be made available to the hardware module through a secure path, delivered on physical media or over an independent electronic path. The signature verification public key must also be made available in a manner that preserves its integrity and confirms its source. CMS supports the transfer of certificates, and that facility can be used to transfer the firmware-signing certificate, but it introduces a level of indirection, so ultimately a trust anchor public key must be made available to the hardware module.

Hardware modules may not be able to reach certificate repositories or delegated path discovery servers, so it is the responsibility of the firmware package signer to include sufficient certificates to let each module validate the firmware-signer certificate. They may also not be able to reach a certificate revocation list repository or an OCSP responder, so if the signature cannot be validated solely with the trust anchor public key and the module cannot perform full certification path validation, then the entity loading the package has to validate the certification path beforehand.

Hardware modules only accept firmware packages with a valid digital signature, either validated directly with the trust anchor public key or through a certification path that ends at the trust anchor. The trust anchors therefore define the set of entities that can create firmware packages for the module.
sections.plainLanguage: The package itself is just a lump of code that the specification treats as opaque, so it does not care how the vendor formats it. What it cares about is the wrapper: the code is squeezed smaller, optionally encrypted, and then signed. The signature is what lets the device tell the vendor's code from someone else's.

sections.title: The Architecture
sections.content:
The architecture includes the hardware module, the firmware package and a bootstrap loader. The bootstrap loader must have access to one or more trusted public keys, called trust anchors, to validate the signature on the firmware package. If a signed firmware package load receipt or error report is created on behalf of the hardware module, the bootstrap loader must also have access to a private signature key and the signer identifier for the corresponding signature validation certificate or its designator, and a signature validation certificate may be included to aid signature validation. To implement that optional capability the hardware module must have a unique serial number and a private signature key, and it may also include a certificate holding the corresponding public key. These items must be installed in the hardware module before it is deployed, and the key and certificate can be generated and installed as part of the manufacture process.

ASN.1 object identifiers are the preferred means of naming the architectural elements. Details of managing the trust anchors are beyond the scope of the specification, but one or more trust anchors must be installed in the hardware module using a secure process before it is deployed, and they provide the means of controlling the acceptable sources of firmware packages. The hardware module vendor can include provisions for secure remote management of trust anchors, and one approach is to include trust anchors in the firmware packages themselves, which is analogous to the optional capability for updating the bootstrap loader.

Many different vendors develop hardware modules, and each vendor typically identifies its modules by product type and revision level, so a unique object identifier must name each hardware module type and revision. Each hardware module within a family should have a unique permanent serial number, and if the optional receipt or error report generation capability is implemented then the module must have one. If a serial number is present, the bootstrap loader uses it for authorization decisions, receipt generation and error report generation. When the module includes more than one firmware-programmable component, the bootstrap loader distributes components of the package to the appropriate components after the package has been validated.

Two approaches to naming firmware packages are supported, legacy and preferred, and the names are placed in a CMS signed attribute rather than in the package itself. A legacy name is simply an octet string with no assumed structure, which is supported to make it easier for existing configuration management systems to work; the signer and the bootstrap loader are assumed to understand any internal structure in that string and to be able to tell which of two names represents the newer version. A preferred name combines the firmware package object identifier with a version number, where a unique object identifier identifies the collection of features that characterise the package, and the version number identifies a particular build or release and must be a monotonically increasing non-negative integer.

The firmware package digital signature must bind the list of supported hardware module object identifiers to the package. The package may also contain a list of community identifiers, which name the hardware modules authorised to load it, and if it does then the bootstrap loader must reject the package when the module is not a member of one of the identified communities.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things are involved: the device, the package, and the small program in the device that loads packages. The device holds one or more trusted public keys, and the loader uses them to check the signature. A package also says which model of device it is for and, optionally, which group of devices may install it, and the loader refuses the package if the device does not qualify.

sections.title: The Bootstrap Loader
sections.content:
The bootstrap loader must have access to a physical interface and any related driver or protocol software necessary to obtain a firmware package, and the same interface should be used to deliver receipts and error reports. The loader can be a permanent part of the hardware module, or it can be replaced by loading a firmware package. If it can be loaded by a firmware package, an initial bootstrap loader must be installed in non-volatile memory prior to deployment, and all bootstrap loaders must meet the requirements in this section.

The loader requires access to cryptographic routines, which can be implemented specifically for it or shared with other module features. It must have access to a one-way hash function and digital signature verification routines, to validate the signature on the package and the certification path for the firmware-signing certificate. If packages are encrypted it must have access to a decryption routine; access to a corresponding encryption function is not required, since hardware modules need not be capable of generating firmware packages. If packages are compressed it must also have access to a decompression function, again with no need for the corresponding compression function.

One or more trust anchors must be installed in non-volatile memory prior to deployment, and the loader must reject a firmware package if it cannot validate the signature, which may require constructing a valid certification path from the firmware-signing certificate to one of the trust anchors. It must also reject a package if the list of supported hardware module type identifiers does not include the object identifier of the hardware module, and it must reject a package that carries a list of community identifiers when the module is not a member of one of the listed communities. It must reject a package if it cannot successfully decrypt it using the firmware-decryption key available to the module; the package carries an identifier of the key needed for decryption.

When an earlier version of a package is replacing a later one, the loader should generate a warning. If a package with a disastrous flaw is released and subsequent versions designate a stale version, the loader should prevent loading of the stale version and of versions earlier than it. For the legacy name form, the stale name is added to a list kept in non-volatile storage when the package is loaded, and later packages are compared against that list, so a new package whose legacy name represents the same version or an older version of a member of the list is rejected. For the preferred name form, the object identifier and the stale version number are kept in non-volatile storage, and a new package is rejected when its object identifier matches and its version number is less than or equal to the stale version number.

The document also deals with packages that depend on one another. The firmware package must identify the package identifiers, and the minimum version numbers when the preferred name form is used, of the packages it depends on, and the loader must reject a load if a dependency is not available. It must also reject a load if the dependencies of any package in the resulting configuration would be unsatisfied. A complete package load is recommended, because incremental loading forces each package to identify its dependencies and the loader to verify them, and because on a general purpose processor it is dangerous to allow arbitrary packages to be loaded simultaneously unless there is a reference monitor.
sections.plainLanguage: The loader is the part that decides. It checks the signature against the stored trusted keys, checks that the package is meant for this model of device, checks the community list if there is one, decrypts it if needed, and refuses to install an old version that the vendor has marked as flawed. It also refuses a package whose dependencies are not present, and refuses one whose installation would break the dependencies of a package already installed.

sections.title: Protecting the Firmware Package
sections.content:
CMS is used to protect a firmware package, which is treated as an opaque binary object. The CMS ContentInfo content type must always be present, and it must encapsulate the CMS SignedData content type. If the package is encrypted, SignedData must encapsulate the CMS EncryptedData content type. If the package is compressed, then either SignedData, when encryption is not used, or EncryptedData, when encryption is used, must encapsulate the CMS CompressedData content type. Finally, SignedData, when neither encryption nor compression is used, EncryptedData, when encryption is used but compression is not, or CompressedData, when compression is used, must encapsulate the simple firmware package using the FirmwarePkgData content type.

Several fields are fixed. The ContentInfo contentType field must carry the id-signedData object identifier, 1.2.840.113549.1.7.2, and the content field must hold SignedData. The SignedData version must be 3, its digestAlgorithms collection must contain a single message digest algorithm identifier, the one employed by the signer, and its signerInfos collection must contain exactly one SignerInfo. The SignerInfo version must be 3 as well, and its signedAttrs collection is required for the firmware package, even though it is optional in CMS, and implementations must ignore unrecognised signed attributes.

The certificates field is optional. If the trust anchor signed the package directly then certificates should be omitted, and otherwise they should include the X.509 certificate of the signer and be sufficient for the loader to build a certification path from the trust anchor to the signer's certificate. PKCS#6 extended certificates and attribute certificates must not be included. The crls field is optional and CRLs should not be included by the signer, because firmware packages are often generated, signed and placed in repositories well before they are downloaded, so it would be difficult to include timely CRLs; but because CRLs are not covered by the signature, timely ones may be inserted by another party before delivery.

The EncryptedData version must be 0 and its unprotectedAttrs field must not be present. The EncryptedContentInfo contentType must be id-ct-compressedData, 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.9, or id-ct-firmwarePackage, 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.16, and its encryptedContent field, although optional in CMS, must be present. The CompressedData version must be 0, and the EncapsulatedContentInfo it holds must have the eContentType id-ct-firmwarePackage. The FirmwarePkgData content type is a straightforward encapsulation in an octet string that need not be DER encoded, and it is identified by the id-ct-firmwarePackage object identifier, 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.16.

The document also specifies the encoding rules. Digitally signed structures must be encoded with the Distinguished Encoding Rules, which are a subset of the Basic Encoding Rules that ensure a single way to represent a given value, because the flexibility of BER is not desirable when digital signatures are used. Other structures do not require DER, but definite length encoding is strongly recommended, so that the bootstrap loader has fewer options to implement.
sections.plainLanguage: The wrapper always has the same shape: a signed message at the top, then optionally an encrypted layer, then optionally a compressed layer, and the raw package at the bottom. Most of the fields are pinned down so that two implementations produce byte-identical results, because a signature covers the exact bytes.

sections.title: The Signed Attributes
sections.content:
The firmware package signer must digitally sign a collection of attributes along with the firmware package, and each attribute must be DER encoded. The SignedAttributes syntax is a set of attributes, and it must include only one instance of any particular attribute.

Four attributes must be present: content-type, message-digest, firmware-package-identifier and target-hardware-module-identifiers. If the package is encrypted, the decrypt-key-identifier attribute must also be present. If the package is intended for use only by specific communities, the community-identifiers attribute must also be present. If the package implements cryptographic algorithms, the implemented-crypto-algorithms attribute may be present, and similarly for compression algorithms. If the package depends on the presence of one or more other packages to operate properly, the firmware-package-info attribute should also be present, for example to indicate a dependency on a particular bootstrap loader or separation kernel. The signer should also include firmware-package-message-digest, signing-time and content-hints, and, if the signer has a certificate, the signing-certificate attribute.

The content-type attribute must carry id-encryptedData, id-ct-compressedData or id-ct-firmwarePackage, according to what was done before signing. The message-digest attribute holds the message digest computed over the eContent octet string, which is the package as it was signed, whether compressed, encrypted or both. The firmware-package-identifier attribute names the protected package and carries either the legacy or the preferred name, optionally together with a stale name or version. The target-hardware-module-identifiers attribute names the types of module the package supports, and the loader must reject the package if its own type identifier is not listed. The decrypt-key-identifier attribute names the symmetric key needed to decrypt the package, with no particular structure imposed on the identifier.

The implemented-crypto-algorithms attribute names the cryptographic algorithms implemented by the package and available to applications, and only those made available at the interface of the module are listed; an algorithm used internally and not accessible through the interface must not be listed.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the facts about the package that the signature covers. Four are always there: what kind of content it is, its digest, its name and version, and the list of device models it fits. The others are added when they apply, such as which key is needed to decrypt it or which group of devices may install it.

sections.title: Firmware Package Load Receipt
sections.content:
In some cases hardware modules can generate receipts to acknowledge the loading of a particular firmware package, and such receipts can be used to determine which modules need to receive an updated package whenever a flaw in an earlier package is discovered. Hardware modules can also generate error reports to indicate unsuccessful loading. To implement either, the hardware module is required to have a unique permanent serial number, and receipts and error reports can be either signed or unsigned. To generate digitally signed receipts or error reports, a hardware module must be issued its own private signature key and a certificate containing the corresponding public key. To save memory in the module, it might store a certificate designator instead of the certificate itself, and the private signature key requires secure storage.

The load receipt has its own CMS content type profile, built on the same ContentInfo and SignedData structure, with a FirmwarePackageLoadReceipt content type inside. Its signed attributes follow the same pattern as the rest of the specification, each with a single attribute value and each present at most once, and the module must include the content-type and message-digest attributes. If the module includes a real-time clock, it should also include the signing-time attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The device can send a note back saying which package it loaded. That note is useful when a flaw is found later, because it shows which devices are still running the bad code. The note can carry the device's serial number, and it can be signed so that the sender of the note can be checked.

sections.title: Firmware Package Load Error
sections.content:
The load error report has the same shape: a CMS ContentInfo wrapping a SignedData whose encapsulated content is a FirmwarePackageLoadError content type, carrying the current firmware configuration and an error code. The report is signed by the hardware module using the same signed attribute pattern, and the module must include the content-type attribute with the value id-ct-firmwareLoadError, 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.18, and the message-digest attribute holding the digest of the error content. If the module includes a real-time clock it should also include the signing-time attribute.

The document lists the error codes, which cover the ways a load can fail. decodeFailure means the ASN.1 decode of the package failed, because the input did not conform to BER or was not ASN.1 at all. badContentInfo, badSignedData, badEncapContent, badCertificate, badSignerInfo, badSignedAttrs and badUnsignedAttrs each mean that the corresponding structure has invalid syntax or carries an unknown or unsupported version. missingContent means the optional eContent is missing where this specification requires it. noTrustAnchor means the signer's key does not lead to an installed trust anchor, and notAuthorized means it does lead to one, but that trust anchor is not an authorised firmware package signer. badDigestAlgorithm, badSignatureAlgorithm and unsupportedKeySize mean the algorithms or key size used by the signer are unknown, unsupported or not usable. signatureFailure means the signature itself could not be validated.

contentTypeMismatch means the content type inside the message does not match the one in the signed attribute. badEncryptedData and unprotectedAttrsPresent cover a malformed EncryptedData structure or the presence of unprotected attributes, which are not permitted. badEncryptContent, badEncryptAlgorithm and missingCiphertext cover a malformed or unsupported encryption setup, and noDecryptKey and decryptFailure cover a missing key and a failed decryption. badCompressAlgorithm, missingCompressedContent and decompressFailure cover the compression layer in the same way. wrongHardware means the processing module is not in the target hardware module identifiers attribute, stalePackage means the package was rejected because it is stale, and notInCommunity means the module is not a member of a listed community. unsupportedPackageType means the package type is not supported by the combination of module and loader, missingDependency and wrongDependencyVersion mean a required package is absent or too old, and insufficientMemory means the module did not have enough memory. badFirmware means the signature validated but the package itself was not in an acceptable format. unsupportedParameters means the signer used signature algorithm parameters the module cannot handle, breaksDependency means another package has a dependency that the new load would break, and otherError covers anything else.
sections.plainLanguage: When a load fails, the device can send back a reason from a fixed list, so that whoever distributed the package knows whether it was refused because the signature did not check out, because the package was for a different model, because it was too old, or because the device ran out of memory.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the document describes the use of CMS to protect firmware packages, the security considerations discussed in the CMS specification apply as well. The conventions it specifies raise a few more of their own.

Private signature keys must be protected. Compromise of the private key used to sign firmware packages permits unauthorised parties to generate packages that hardware modules will accept, and compromise of the hardware module private key allows unauthorised parties to generate signed load receipts and error reports. The firmware-decryption key must also be protected, because compromise of that key may result in the disclosure of the firmware package.

Cryptographic algorithms become weaker with time, and the ability to change the firmware package is an opportunity to update or replace them. That capability is desirable, but algorithm replacement can lead to interoperability failures, so the rollout of new algorithms must be managed: generally the previous generation and its replacement need to be supported at the same time to allow an orderly transition.

Random number generation matters. When packages are encrypted, the source must randomly generate the encryption keys, and generating signature key pairs relies on random numbers too. An inadequate pseudo-random number generator can result in little or no security, because an attacker may find it much easier to reproduce the generator's state and search the resulting small set of possibilities than to search the whole key space.

The stale version number is a policy choice for the signer, and the document sets out when it is useful. It is especially useful when the security interests of the person choosing which version to load do not align with those of the signer, for example in hardware modules that provide digital rights management, when the deployment organisation rather than the vendor is the signer, and for devices employed by the military. The mechanism cannot completely prevent subsequent use of the stale package: by loading different types of package, each with its own stale version number, until the internal storage for stale version numbers is exceeded, the user can circumvent it. The legacy name form does not improve the situation, because legacy names are usually larger than an object identifier, so comparable protection needs more memory. A signer can make sure that stale version numbers are honoured by limiting the number of different types of package it signs, so that every module can store a stale version number for each type.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things decide whether this scheme holds up: the signing key must stay secret, the encryption key must stay secret, and the key generation must use good random numbers. The document is also honest that the anti-rollback feature can be worked around by cycling through enough different package types to fill the module's storage, which is why the signer is advised to sign only a few types.

ContentInfo
  SignedData                      always present
    EncapsulatedContentInfo
      EncryptedData                 only when encrypted

items.label: Not ASN.1
items.desc: The decode of the firmware package failed.

items.label: No trust anchor
items.desc: The signer's key does not lead to an installed trust anchor.

items.label: Not an authorised signer
items.desc: The trust anchor reached is not an authorised firmware package signer.

items.label: Signature did not verify
items.desc: The signature in the SignerInfo could not be validated.

items.label: No decryption key
items.desc: The module does not have the key named in the decrypt key identifier.

items.label: Wrong device
items.desc: The processing module is not listed in the target hardware module identifiers.

items.label: Stale package
items.desc: The package was rejected because it is stale.

items.label: Not in a listed community
items.desc: The module is not a member of the community named in the community identifiers.

items.label: Not enough memory
items.desc: The package could not be loaded because the module lacked sufficient memory.

viz.caption: WHAT THE DOCUMENT SAYS ABOUT SECURITY (RFC 4108)

items.title: Protect the signing key
items.text: Compromise of the key used to sign packages lets anyone produce packages the module will accept.

items.title: Protect the decryption key
items.text: Compromise of the firmware-decryption key can disclose the package to unauthorised parties.

items.title: Use good random numbers
items.text: A weak pseudo-random generator can make the key space small enough to search.

items.title: Roll out new algorithms carefully
items.text: The old and new generations usually have to be supported at the same time to avoid interoperability failures.

items.title: The anti-rollback limit
items.text: The stale version feature can be worked around by loading enough different package types to fill the module's storage.
